theorem_conditions.hypotheses: The frozen snapshot has an empty literature history and no attempt records. The supplied auxiliary-results artifact says its arguments were authored and sequentially reviewed in one host session, while expressly disclaiming independent AI review, external referee review, and formal proof-assistant checking.

theorem_conditions.hypotheses: Two distinct nonzero integer elements have opposite signs, and their product plus one is a rational square.
theorem_conditions.reasoning: Their integer product is at most -1. Since the product plus one is nonnegative, the product is at least -1 and therefore equals -1; the pair is {-1,1}. Negating every element preserves pairwise products, so the other integer-anchor case can be represented by positive integer anchors, without implying that the remaining elements are positive. For any additional element x paired with both exceptional anchors, x+1 and 1-x are nonnegative squares; hence -1 ≤ x ≤ 1, and distinctness from the anchors makes both inequalities strict. There is no third distinct nonzero integer in that interval.
theorem_conditions.conclusion: The sign reduction and the stated limitation on the signs of the other elements follow. They do not decide whether four additional rational elements can satisfy all required edges.

theorem_conditions.claim: Proposed target A: denominator and divisibility conclusions for common neighbors of {-1,1}
theorem_conditions.location: Snapshot inline artifact, proposed target A; the parametrization is also given in its historical reduction paragraph.
theorem_conditions.hypotheses: For primitive integers m,n with n>0, m≠0 and m≠±n, set q=m²+n² and F(m/n)=4mn(n²-m²)/q².
theorem_conditions.reasoning: For every odd prime p dividing q, p divides neither m nor n. If p divided n²-m² as well, it would divide 2m² and hence m, a contradiction. Thus no odd prime factor of q cancels against the numerator. If q is even, primitiveness forces m,n odd; q≡2 mod 8 and n²-m² is divisible by 8, so the only cancellation at 2 against q² is a factor 4. The reduced denominator is therefore (q/gcd(q,2))². Every odd prime p dividing q has -1 as a square modulo p, since (m/n)²≡-1 mod p, so p≡1 mod 4. The positive square root q/gcd(q,2) is at least 5: the only possible smaller q for nonzero primitive m,n is q=2, which has m=±n and is excluded. The numerator is divisible by 24. For divisibility by 8, if q is odd then m,n have opposite parity and mn is even; if q is even, m,n are odd and n²-m² is divisible by 8. For divisibility by 3, either 3 divides mn or the nonzero squares m²,n² agree modulo 3. In the even-q case cancellation by 4 leaves a numerator divisible by 8, and q is not divisible by 3, so the reduced numerator remains divisible by 24.
theorem_conditions.conclusion: The stated denominator formula, lower bound 25, odd-prime restriction on its square root, and reduced-numerator divisibility by 24 hold for the specified primitive parameters and either sign of m.

theorem_conditions.claim: Proposed target B: fixed finite local square tests do not obstruct the {-1,1} candidate family
theorem_conditions.location: Snapshot inline artifact, proposed target B.
theorem_conditions.hypotheses: Let S be any finite set of primes, P its product (P=1 if S is empty), and M=P. Choose arbitrarily large positive L≡1 mod P and set t_i=iP/L for i=1,2,3,4. Take L sufficiently large that the t_i lie in an interval (0,ε) where F(t)=4t(1-t²)/(1+t²)² is strictly increasing and 0<F(t)<1.
theorem_conditions.reasoning: There are infinitely many such L. Strict increase makes the four x_i=F(t_i) distinct and in (0,1); as L increases in this range, x_1 strictly decreases, giving infinitely many distinct sets. The identities 1+F(t)=((t²-2t-1)/(1+t²))² and 1-F(t)=((1-2t-t²)/(1+t²))² give rational-square edges from every x_i to both anchors; the edge between -1 and 1 has value zero, also a rational square. For p∈S, L is a p-adic unit and v_p(t_i)≥1. The factors 1±t_i² are units, so v_p(x_i)≥1 for odd p and v_2(x_i)=2+v_2(t_i)≥3 for p=2. Consequently v_p(x_ix_j)≥1 for odd p and v_2(x_ix_j)≥3. For odd p, 1+y with v_p(y)≥1 has a square root in Q_p by Hensel lifting the simple root 1 modulo p. For p=2, v_2(y)≥3 gives 1+y≡1 mod 8; every such unit is a square in Q_2. One elementary lifting argument starts with an odd root modulo 8 and, at each stage k≥3, adjusts a root modulo 2^k by either 0 or 2^(k-1) to match the next bit modulo 2^(k+1). Applying these facts to y=x_ix_j proves the six remaining edge values are squares in every Q_p for p∈S.
theorem_conditions.conclusion: For any fixed finite S, infinitely many distinct candidates with anchors {-1,1} satisfy the global rational-square anchor edges and the six remaining edges are squares in every Q_p for p∈S. This is a finite-local-test barrier only: it does not give rational square roots for those six edges.

theorem_conditions.claim: Limits of the supplied auxiliary results
theorem_conditions.location: Auxiliary results L2-L5 and “Remaining main-goal obligations.”
theorem_conditions.hypotheses: The main objective quantifies over every allowable rational height and integer pair and requires all fifteen pairwise product-plus-one conditions.
theorem_conditions.conclusion: L2's common-neighbor parametrization and infinite-graph K4 formulation are not an all-height obstruction. L3's square-denominator conclusion requires coprime integer anchors; its counterexample demonstrates why the hypothesis matters. L4 concerns only the specified canonical point of order exactly three in a triple and does not cover other placements of integers in a sextuple. L5 gives false positives for a preliminary extension test, not a proof that the displayed quadruples have no other extensions. None resolves existence or nonexistence of the target sextuple.

unresolved_items: Existence or nonexistence of a rational D(1) sextuple with at least two integers remains unresolved, both in the all-positive case and with unrestricted signs.

For opposite-sign integer anchors, reduction to {-1,1} and the common-neighbor parametrization do not decide whether four distinct nonzero rational common neighbors can satisfy all six mutual rational-square conditions.
For positive integer anchors, no obstruction covering every integer pair and unbounded rational heights is supplied; the infinite K4 criterion is not reduced to a finite search.

The proposed target A's phrase “numerator/denominator prime restrictions are exact” is underspecified beyond the verified denominator formula and numerator divisibility by 24; any stronger intended classification remains unaudited.
Target B defeats every fixed finite set of p-adic square tests in its stated setting, but does not extend local square roots to rational square roots or settle the global sextuple problem.
The supplied references to DKMS, arXiv:1507.00569, and DKP, JNT 205 (2019), were not independently checked; exact passages and any literature claims depending on them remain unresolved.
